variants.name: Typed accessor caching a Promise
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types, not mechanics: the deferral is the same accessor plus cached promise as JavaScript, typed as Promise<Author> (or Author | undefined for a synchronously loaded cache), and private/readonly express intent at compile time only. The type system can make the deferral explicit in the API shape - a getter returning Promise<Author>, or a small Lazy<T> wrapper class - but it cannot stop an accessor from hitting the store; for entities mapped by an ORM, the ORM's lazy relation (sibling variant) is the declarative form.
pitfalls: A cached rejected promise sticks until the field is reset, and private fields are invisible to JSON serialization: choose retry vs cache explicitly and project to a DTO shape instead of serializing the entity.
Getters that load turn loops into N+1 queries: prefetch with relation options or a batched loader where the use case walks many parents.
A missing load looks like an empty value (await book.author giving undefined); type the accessor so absence is explicit, for example Promise<Author | null>.

variants.name: TypeORM Promise-typed lazy relation
variants.implementation_notes: TypeORM lets the relation itself carry the marker: a relation declared with a Promise type ('@ManyToOne(() => Author) author!: Promise<Author>;') is loaded when it is accessed - the documentation describes the property as storing the value in a promise that resolves on access - so the find options stay free of the relation. Choose it when entities are loaded through a repository/query builder and the domain tolerates promise-typed navigations; plain objects and some query-builder paths bypass the proxy, and prefetching remains the answer for loops.
variants.idiom_name: TypeORM lazy relation (@ManyToOne with Promise-typed property)
pitfalls: Promise-typed navigations only work on entities materialised by the ORM: a plain object or deserialized DTO awaits a non-promise and fails or yields undefined.
Every navigation becomes asynchronous: business methods must turn async, and loops over relations become N+1 unless relations are prefetched.
